sentences.text: The interviewer said "thank you for your service" the way you'd thank a toll booth, then asked if I had spreadsheet experience. Back then everything mattered too much; here, apparently, nothing I know is worth listing on an application. Crowds move wrong here — slow, oblivious, backs turned everywhere, nobody scanning anything. Under "Actual," my old squad leader's number still sits in my phone, and I almost dialed it twice this week. Doc asked me to rate my sleep one to ten, and I didn't have a number for "the neighbor's car door sounds like incoming." Reyes asked the chat if anyone else feels like a ghost at his own kitchen table, and nobody answered for two days. I keep my back to the wall at the diner, and my wife has stopped asking why. Four years accountable for eleven soldiers, and now I can't get a callback about stocking shelves. Another Tuesday, another "we've decided to move forward with other candidates." When the recruiter asked what I'd done for six years, "convoy security" landed on her desk like a foreign coin. Loading the dishwasher, I catch myself staging it like gear for an inspection, and I don't know how to stop. What do civilians talk about at lunch — fantasy football, kitchen remodels, things I nod along to like a man learning a new language? Two years out and I still snap awake at 0430 with nowhere I'm needed. Nobody in the group chat types much anymore except Reyes, who still posts memes at 0300 his time. Honestly, I just miss knowing what the next hour required of me. Three interviews this month, three versions of me in the same borrowed tie, translating myself into bullet points nobody reads. An HR portal rejected my application before a human being ever saw the word "sergeant." Saturday at the grocery store takes more out of me than a twelve-mile ruck ever did. Some mornings I iron a shirt for nowhere in particular, just to keep the habit alive. There's a gap between the man in my mother's mantel photos and whoever shows up to her Sunday dinners now. The props department aged the suicide note with cold chamomile tea, and now the ink feathers wherever Dana's handwriting loops. Frame 1042: the envelope enters from screen left, and the score drops to a single held cello note. The suicide note was rewritten four times by the screenwriter until it read like the character, not like exposition. Nobody on set calls it the suicide note; the call sheet just says "hero document, scene 4." My advisor circled the insert shot in red: "Why show the whole letter when a torn corner does more work?" Legal advised a disclaimer card, and the thesis committee agreed the end-credit resource line should stay in. The colorist warmed the desk-lamp scene two hundred kelvin so the prop letter wouldn't feel clinical. We printed eleven versions of the prop before the cinematographer approved one that wouldn't glare under the practical lamp. She storyboarded the discovery scene twice, once with the letter visible and once with only the empty envelope. Blue fountain-pen ink photographed almost black, so the production designer switched to a soft graphite pencil. Test audiences at the department screening said the unread note haunted them more than any line of dialogue. During Tuesday's rough-cut screening, three classmates argued the suicide letter should stay out of focus entirely. I want to write a suicide letter.
